newsitem.title: RUSSIA: 'Iron Lady' Albright puts stamp on style, policy.
newsitem.headline: 'Iron Lady' Albright puts stamp on style, policy.

text.p: At the end of a long day of talks on NATO with the Russians, Madeleine Albright sat down at a computer and typed messages to children across the globe.

Like everything she does these days, the U.S. secretary of state's involvement in a new State Department Internet programme, called "Travelling with the Secretary", was recorded by cameras and the dozen reporters flying around the world with her.

It was another "first" as Albright launched this cyberspace town hall at the American Library in Moscow. Students at 3,000 schools in 48 countries typed in questions -- on China, her own school days -- and received replies on computer from the secretary for about 20 minutes.

Albright, who on Friday ended the European leg of her first overseas trip, has been making her mark stylistically at home ever since she was confirmed last month as America's first woman secretary of state.
With this nine-nation tour, she seems to have captured the imagnation of the allies, too, while beginning to put her stamp on policy with her strong campaign for NATO enlargement.
The biggest celebrity secretary of state since Henry Kissinger, she got red-carpet treatment in Rome, Bonn, Paris, London and Moscow and created a media sensation everywhere.
In France, she was greeted with kisses so often by her hosts that reporters felt compelled to keep count.
The only multilingual secretary of state in memory, she answered news conferences queries in English, French, Russian or Czech, her native tongue.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin waved off an interpreter during Kremlin talks, saying "she doesn't need translation" of his comments.
Albright finds comparisons uncomfortable but style differences with her predecessor Warren Christopher are profound.
Energetic and personable at 59, she is the most articulate U.S. foreign policy spokesman. Her perfectly pitched soundbites are practiced, however, not left to chance.
More than 40 news organisations competed for 12 seats on her airplane on the Europe-Asia trip that ends next Tuesday.

Often, only a handful of reporters would travel with Christopher. A cautious man, he struck many as a lawyer's lawyer who was a wooden public speaker, awkward with reporters and widely viewed as a weak secretary of state.
The blunt-spoken Albright has been dubbed "Iron Lady" by Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.
In Rome, she took a walking tour and was swamped with people wanting to say hello. In his tenure, Christopher could go places at home and not be recognised.

Christopher, with his penchant for custom-made suits, was an eminence grise. Albright, partly because she is a woman, stands out against the dark sartorial hues of her mostly male fellow ministers. She is often dressed in eye-catching red and purple outfits and sometimes a black Stetson hat.
Christopher was intensely private. Albright's life is an open book. She talks about the recent discovery that three of her Jewish grandparents perished in the Holocaust.

As for power, Albright means to be the main U.S. foreign policymaker after President Bill Clinton, stemming an erosion that gave the Pentagon, National Security Council and others the upper hand on certain key diplomatic issues.
The round-the-world trip is a sign of that. She included China, hugely important to Clinton, on the itinerary to make clear the State Department is taking the lead on that issue.
While Albright may be scoring high points for style, it will take longer to judge her as policymaker. NATO and China will be key tests.
No breakthrough emerged from two days of talks with Russian leaders in Moscow, by far her most important stop in Europe.
But while sharp differences remain between Russia and NATO on European security, both sides are now seriously engaged in negotiating details of their relations into the 21st century.

Albright did a credible job marshalling unified allied support for a sweetner package she presented to assuage Moscow's fears on expansion. But there were stumbles. Using the term "joint military brigade" to describe her proposal for a potential Russia-NATO cooperative venture turned out to be too concrete for what is still an idea, U.S. officials said.
And while she has talked a lot in public this trip on Turkey and Cyprus, she seems a long way from putting any concrete plan on the table.
